subject: chemistry
title: Reacting masses from equations
key_idea: The big numbers in a balanced equation show how many moles of each substance react. To find an unknown mass: convert the known mass to moles, use the equation ratio, then convert the moles of the unknown back to a mass.

blocks.text: A balanced equation can be read as a recipe in moles. This section covers what the numbers in front of the formulae mean.

blocks.label: Magnesium and hydrochloric acid
where: 1 mol of Mg reacts with 2 mol of HCl.
This makes 1 mol of MgCl₂ and 1 mol of H₂.

items: The big numbers are the **mole ratio**. No big number means 1.
The ratio compares moles. It does not compare masses.
In the equation 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO, 2 mol of Mg make 2 mol of MgO, so the ratio Mg : MgO is 1 : 1.
The big numbers in an equation give the mole ratio.
Compare moles, never masses, using the ratio.
No number in front of a formula means 1.

blocks.text: Every reacting-mass question uses the same three steps. The ratio from the equation connects the two substances.

items.text: Starting with 1.35 g of Mg (Ar = 24.0): 1.35 ÷ 24.0 = 0.05625 mol.
2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. The ratio Mg : MgO is 2 : 2, so moles of MgO = 0.05625 mol.

diagram.alt: Practise calculating the mass of magnesium oxide made from a mass of magnesium.
diagram.question: Magnesium burns in oxygen: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. Calculate the maximum mass of magnesium oxide made from **{m} g** of magnesium. (Ar: Mg = 24, O = 16)
working: Mole ratio Mg : MgO = 2 : 2, so moles of MgO are the same

items.text: 3Mg + 2FeCl₃ → 2Fe + 3MgCl₂. Use 0.120 g of Mg to find the mass of Fe (Ar: Mg = 24, Fe = 56).

items: Change kg or tonnes into grams first, and change the answer back if the question asks for it.
A mass-ratio method also works: 48 g of Mg makes 80 g of MgO, so scale up or down.
Multiply by the ratio, big number wanted ÷ big number known.
Check the units asked for in the answer.

checks.q: What does the 2 in 2HCl mean in Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂?
checks.a: Two moles of hydrochloric acid react with each mole of magnesium.

checks.q: Calcium carbonate decomposes: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. Calculate the mass of calcium oxide made from 50.0 g of calcium carbonate. (Mr: CaCO₃ = 100, CaO = 56)
checks.a: Moles of CaCO₃ = 50.0 ÷ 100 = 0.500. The ratio is 1 : 1, so moles of CaO = 0.500. Mass = 0.500 × 56 = 28.0 g.

checks.q: Why can you not just use the masses of the formulae in the equation as a ratio, such as 3 × 24 : 2 × 56?
checks.a: The equation ratio is in moles. Convert to moles using the mass and Mr of the known substance, then use the ratio.

worked_example.question:
This question is about iron.

Magnesium reacts with iron chloride solution.

3 Mg + 2 FeCl₃ → 2 Fe + 3 MgCl₂

0.120 g of magnesium reacts with excess iron chloride solution.

Relative atomic masses (Ar): Mg = 24, Fe = 56

Calculate the mass of iron produced, in mg.
worked_example.tip: One mark each for dividing by 24, using the 2/3 ratio, multiplying by 56, and the two answers.

blocks.text: (AQA: Higher tier) For AQA, this topic is Higher tier only.

worked_example.question:
Magnesium burns in excess oxygen to form magnesium oxide.

The balanced equation for this reaction is

2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO

Starting with 1.35 g of magnesium, calculate the maximum mass of magnesium oxide that could be formed in this reaction.

(relative atomic masses: O = 16.0, Mg = 24.0)

You must show your working.
worked_example.tip: A mass-ratio method also scores: 48 g Mg forms 80 g MgO, so 1.35 g forms 80 ÷ 48 × 1.35 = 2.25 g.

blocks.text: For Edexcel, reacting-mass questions are set at Foundation tier as well. A mass-ratio method is accepted.

items: From 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO: 48 g of Mg forms 80 g of MgO.
1 g of Mg forms 80 ÷ 48 = 1.67 g of MgO.
1.35 g of Mg forms 1.35 × 80 ÷ 48 = 2.25 g of MgO.

worked_example.question:
In another neutralisation reaction dilute sulfuric acid, H₂SO₄, reacts with potassium hydroxide solution, KOH.

H₂SO₄ + 2KOH → K₂SO₄ + 2H₂O

Calculate the mass of potassium sulfate, K₂SO₄, that could be made from 6.54 g of dilute sulfuric acid, H₂SO₄.

Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

Relative atomic mass (Ar): H = 1.0, K = 39.1, O = 16.0, S = 32.1
answer_points: Mr of H₂SO₄ = 98.1 and Mr of K₂SO₄ = 174.3 (1)
worked_example.tip: The ratio of H₂SO₄ to K₂SO₄ is 1 : 1, so the Mr values can be used directly.

blocks.text: For OCR, reacting-mass questions are set in Foundation papers as well. Scaling the masses from the equation is enough.

items: From Cu + Cl₂ → CuCl₂: 63.5 g of Cu makes 134.5 g of CuCl₂.
0.635 g is one hundredth of 63.5 g, so it makes 134.5 ÷ 100 = 1.345 g of CuCl₂.

worked_example.question:
When magnesium nitrate is heated strongly, magnesium oxide is formed. The equation for this reaction is shown.

2Mg(NO₃)₂ → 2MgO + 4NO₂ + O₂

Calculate the volume of NO₂ gas, at r.t.p., formed when 7.40 g of Mg(NO₃)₂ is heated.

Use the following steps.
● Calculate the Mr of Mg(NO₃)₂.
● Calculate the number of moles of Mg(NO₃)₂ used.
● Determine the number of moles of NO₂ formed.
● Calculate the volume of NO₂ gas, in cm³, at r.t.p.

blocks.text: Core questions ask for a reacting mass by simple proportion, without moles. Use the Mr values and the equation to scale the masses.

items.lead: Find the masses in the equation.
items.text: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. Ar: Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16. 100 g of CaCO₃ makes 56 g of CaO.

items.lead: Scale to the mass you have.
items.text: For 25 g of CaCO₃, divide by 100 and multiply by 25. This is a quarter of the amounts.

items: Multiply each Mr by the big number in front of it before you scale.
The masses in the equation are in grams, but any one unit works if you use it for both substances.
(Supplement) For a gas at r.t.p., volume = moles × 24 dm³ (24 000 cm³). One mole of any gas has this volume.

worked_example.question:
Heptane burns completely in oxygen. This is the equation for the complete combustion of heptane.

C₇H₁₆ + 11O₂ → 7CO₂ + 8H₂O

Calculate the minimum mass of oxygen needed for the complete combustion of 30.0 g of heptane.

[for C₇H₁₆, Mr = 100; for O₂, Mr = 32]
worked_example.tip: One mark for each step. Use the ratio of 1 : 11 from the equation, not the masses.
